description.value: We explore neural circuits implicated in social reward processing in individuals with a history of AN who are weight-restored relative to controls and examine the effects of illness course on the experience of social value.

spans.text: We explore neural circuits implicated in social reward processing in individuals with a history of AN who are weight-restored relative to controls and examine the effects of illness course on the experience of social value.

value: We hypothesized that individuals in the AN-WR group will demonstrate diminished activation in reward-related regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and striatum, while viewing social stimuli whether full bodies or smiling faces; ultimately reflecting a generalization of diminished reward valuation beyond disorder-related domains.

Additionally, we hypothesized that individuals in the AN-WR group, despite weight-restoration, will differ in the subjective valuation of attractiveness as a function of weight category relative to control participants (cf. [ 17 ]).

Lastly, we predict that impaired social reward valuation will be worse in individuals with a more stable disorder course, reflecting a process of assigning value that becomes exaggerated with disorder progression, a hypothesis consistent with the model of neuroprogressive changes with illness duration proposed by Treasure, Stein, and Maguire [ 39 ].

description.value: Participants viewed images of faces, described as smiling-face social stimuli, for 2 seconds. On a subset of trials they rated attractiveness using a button box.

Participants viewed full-body images of women with faces visible, spanning emaciated, normal-weight, and overweight/varied attractiveness categories, for 2 seconds. On a subset of trials they rated attractiveness using a button box.
Participants viewed scrambled images of the face and body stimuli for 2 seconds as a visual control condition; attractiveness ratings were made on a subset of trials.

spans.text: We used a mixed blocked/event-related design such that 8 images from each trial type (faces, bodies, scrambled) were presented within each block.
Images were displayed using Neurobehavioral Systems’ Presentation software.

instructions.value: Participants viewed each image for 2 seconds. On 12 trials per run, they rated the image's attractiveness on a 1-to-4 scale using a button box.

stimuli.value: Images of smiling faces, full human body figures with faces visible varying in weight and attractiveness, and scrambled versions of the stimuli used as a visual control.

spans.text: The EDE-Q is a 28-item self-report questionnaire that provides a continuous measure of eating disorder symptomatology and is broken into four subscales: restraint, eating concern, shape concern, and weight concern.

description.value: The 28-item Eating Disorders Examination Questionnaire, version 6, was administered as a continuous measure of eating-disorder symptomatology. It produces restraint, eating concern, shape concern, weight concern, and global scores and was used to characterize eating-disorder symptoms in the groups.

spans.text: MPFC was defined based on our previous neuroimaging work [ 48 ] and previous studies of social cognition and reward processing [ 49 ,  50 ] as a sphere of 25 mm radius encompassing medial regions of Brodmann Area (BA) 9 and 10 and BA32, as well as superior portions of BA14 ( Fig 2 ).
Magnetic resonance images were acquired on a General Electric 3T scanner using a spiral-in pulse sequence.

description.value: Functional MRI data were preprocessed in FSL 4.1.8 using brain extraction with BET, high-pass filtering above 100 seconds, 6-mm FWHM Gaussian spatial smoothing, and motion correction with MCFLIRT. Data were registered from each participant's high-resolution anatomical image to the MNI template using FLIRT.

spans.text: Imaging data were analyzed using a general linear model in FSL, FEAT [ 45 ].
Stimulus onset times were convolved with a standard double-gamma hemodynamic response function, and were corrected for local autocorrelation within a single run [ 46 ].

model_settings.value: First-level FSL FEAT general linear models included separate regressors for faces, bodies, and scrambled images during the 2-second presentation period, plus a nuisance regressor for attractiveness-rating periods. Stimulus onsets were convolved with a standard double-gamma HRF; local autocorrelation was corrected within each run. Participant effects across runs were combined with a fixed-effects model.

spans.text: At the second level, a fixed-effects model was used to combine data from all runs within a single participant.
Third-level group models were analyzed using FSL’s FLAME1 mixed-effects model.

model_settings.value: Third-level group analyses used FSL FLAME1 mixed-effects models. Age was included as a nuisance regressor orthogonalized to each group's mean; illness-course scores were similarly orthogonalized to the clinical group's mean. Analyses were conducted within a priori ROI masks and across the whole brain, with voxel threshold z > 3.1 and cluster-corrected p < 0.05.
